Every discounted-cash-flow valuation rests on two numbers you made up:
a growth forecast and a discount rate, each borrowed from a different
model, neither obliged to agree with the other. This course teaches the
alternative I used to answer one of asset pricing's oldest questions:
derive **both** numbers from a single description of the economy — one
consumption process, one set of preferences — and let the same machine
price every claim, from the aggregate stock market to a portfolio you
bring yourself.

The vehicle is my paper, *Is the Value Premium a Puzzle?* Value firms
have out-earned growth firms by about six percentage points a year over
1930–2003, while their market betas are nearly identical — the CAPM
calls that impossible. By the end of the course you will have rebuilt
the general-equilibrium model that resolves this, tested it against
seventy-four years of data, and used it to price a claim of your own.

## The destination

The table the course builds toward: the model, calibrated to
consumption and dividends alone — no return ever enters — confronted
with the returns it was never shown. Data columns are the paper's
prints (Table I and Table VII); model columns are computed live when
this page builds.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
import lrrcs as lrr

solver = lrr.ModelSolver(lrr.get_table_ii_params(), n_x=30, n_s=4).solve()
tab = lrr.simulate_table_vii(solver, n_samples=300, years=74, seed=0)

data_er = {"growth": 7.81, "value": 13.88, "market": 8.56}   # Kiku, Table I
print(f"{'':10s} {'E[R] data':>10s} {'E[R] model':>11s}")
for name in ("growth", "value", "market"):
    print(f"{name:10s} {data_er[name]:10.2f} {tab['mean_return'][name]:11.2f}")
print(f"\nvalue premium: about 6 in the data, "
      f"{tab['value_premium']:.1f} in the model")
print(f"CAPM beta ratio (value/growth): {tab['beta_ratio']:.2f} "
      f"— lower beta, higher return: the anomaly, reproduced")
```

## The argument, in order

**Part I — The Puzzle.** A DCF has [two free numbers](chapters/01-two-free-numbers.qmd);
fixing them honestly requires a model of risk. The
[data](chapters/02-value-premium-in-the-data.qmd): six points of premium
the CAPM cannot price.

**Part II — The Toolkit.** One equation prices everything
([the Euler equation](chapters/03-pricing-by-euler-equation.qmd));
[Epstein–Zin preferences](chapters/04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) make
news about the future priced today; a
[long-run risks endowment](chapters/05-long-run-risks.qmd) supplies the
news.

**Part III — Solving.** The
[log-linear solution](chapters/06-log-linear-solution.qmd) in closed
form, then the [quadrature solution](chapters/07-quadrature-solution.qmd)
without approximation — and what each hides.

**Part IV — Confronting the Data.**
[Calibrate cash flows](chapters/08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd) with no
return in sight; test the [market](chapters/09-the-market-test.qmd);
watch the [value premium resolve](chapters/10-value-premium-resolved.qmd)
with nothing re-tuned.

**Part V — Your Turn.**
[Price your own claim](chapters/11-price-your-own-claim.qmd), then read
the [objections and the model's honest limits](chapters/12-objections-and-limits.qmd).

New here? Start with [How to read this course](how-to-read.qmd). The
claim throughout is not that this model is true — it is that a
valuation should get its forecast and its discount rate from one
place, and this is the cleanest working example.
